analysis.one_liner: Imposes passenger protections on airlines: delay refunds, cancellation compensation, baggage liability, and competition rules.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a vote: it sat in an aviation subcommittee after two May 1991 hearings until the Congress ended in January 1993.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have required airlines to tell passengers about long delays and offer refunds, banned most flight cancellations within 72 hours of departure (with compensation when violated), set a $2,500 minimum liability for lost or damaged bags, sped up baggage claims, published airline-by-airline service quality rankings, and protected ticket holders when an airline went bankrupt. It also targeted competition problems: it would have let airports charge peak-hour landing fees, subjected hub gate deals to antitrust review, regulated the computer reservation systems then owned by the biggest airlines, and restricted transfers of route certificates. It never left the House aviation subcommittee.
analysis.who_benefits: Airline passengers gain the most: people facing long delays would get notice and a refund offer, passengers on economically canceled flights would get denied-boarding-style compensation, travelers with lost or damaged bags would have a $2,500 minimum claim and a 60-day decision deadline, and holders of tickets on bankrupt airlines could fly space-available on other carriers at no charge. Travelers also gain from honest fare advertising, transferable nonrefundable tickets, published service-quality rankings, and easier complaint filing with the Transportation Department.

how_it_helps.text: Airlines must notify passengers of delays of one hour or more and offer a refund of the ticket price before boarding.
Airlines cannot cancel a scheduled flight within 72 hours of departure for any reason other than safety or no passengers, and must compensate ticket holders when they do.
Airlines may not cap baggage liability below $2,500, must decide lost-bag claims within 60 days, and are responsible for bags mishandled by their code-sharing partners.
If an airline goes bankrupt and stops flying a route, other carriers serving that route must carry its ticket holders space-available at no extra charge.

The Transportation Department must publish quarterly rankings of airlines on on-time performance, cancellations, missed connections, mishandled baggage, bumping, and complaints, and set up offices at hub airports to take passenger complaints.
Nonrefundable tickets and tickets with cancellation penalties must be transferable from one passenger to another, and fare ads must disclose restrictions.

analysis.who_pays: Airlines bear the costs: refunds and cancellation compensation, higher baggage liability and faster claim processing, civil penalties up to $100,000 per illegal economic cancellation and $10,000 per reporting violation, and new monthly reporting on delays, missed connections, cancellations, and baggage. Owners of computer reservation systems lose contractual advantages, and hub airport gate deals face Justice Department antitrust review.

drawbacks.text: Compliance costs for airlines—refunds, cancellation compensation, higher baggage liability, and civil penalties—would likely be passed on to travelers through higher fares.

The 72-hour cancellation ban reaches beyond 'economic' cancellations to any nonsafety cancellation, which could force airlines to fly nearly empty planes or delay schedule adjustments, and the bill acknowledges this by carving out safety-related schedule changes.

The bill relies heavily on new Transportation Department rulemaking and reporting—monthly performance lists, service rankings, complaint offices at hubs—adding regulatory machinery whose effectiveness depends on aggressive enforcement.
The civil penalty provision lets the Secretary consider an airline's ability to pay when setting fines, which could soften enforcement against large carriers.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The passenger protections are concrete and would have addressed problems travelers face directly: surprise delays, cancellations without compensation, lowball baggage payouts, and stranded tickets when an airline fails. The main honest objection is cost: airlines would pass refund, compensation, and liability expenses into fares, and the 72-hour cancellation ban is blunt, potentially forcing wasteful operations. The competition provisions—peak-hour fees, antitrust review of hub gate agreements, and rules for the airline-owned computer reservation systems—were aimed at real concentration in the industry. On balance the bill was designed to shift leverage from airlines to passengers, with costs that are real but modest relative to a multi-billion-dollar industry.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was sent to the House Public Works and Transportation Committee, then to its aviation subcommittee, which held two hearings in May 1991—but it was never reported out of committee and never came up for a vote before the Congress ended in January 1993.

narrative.text: Rep. John Paul Hammerschmidt (R-AR) introduced the Airline Competition and Passenger Protection Act of 1991 on April 24, 1991, with 8 cosponsors split evenly between 4 Republicans and 4 Democrats.
The House referred the bill to the Committee on Public Works and Transportation on April 24, 1991, and to the Subcommittee on Aviation on May 6, 1991.
The Aviation Subcommittee held hearings on May 15 and May 22, 1991, but the bill never advanced to a full committee vote or to the House floor.
The 102nd Congress ended on January 3, 1993, and the bill died in committee without any vote.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Airlines were better off: none of the refund, compensation, baggage-liability, reporting, penalty, or competition requirements ever took effect. Passengers gained nothing from the bill's death, and the service and competition problems it targeted continued without these federal protections.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Airlines, which faced no new rules

industries.note: The bill would have cost airlines through refund offers, compensation for economic cancellations, a $2,500 baggage liability floor with 60-day claim deadlines, monthly performance reporting, and civil penalties up to $100,000 per violation—all protections travelers would have gained. Airlines' interest in blocking it ran directly against passengers' interest in the protections.

industries.industry: Computer reservation system owners (then mostly the largest airlines)
industries.note: The bill ordered a final rule to eliminate the anticompetitive effects of computer reservation systems—contract lock-ins, fees on non-owning carriers, and display bias—which would have ended advantages the system owners held over both rival airlines and travel agents booking for travelers.

Airports could charge nondiscriminatory peak-hour landing fees to cut congestion, a tool for reducing delays, while gate and facility agreements with dominant carriers became subject to Justice Department competition review.
